contentBlocks.text: You've learned power-of-a-power and the zero exponent. Today: what a negative exponent actually means!

A negative exponent means take the reciprocal: x⁻ⁿ = 1/xⁿ. This follows from the quotient rule too — x²/x⁵ = x⁻³ using the rule, but expanding it directly gives 1/x³, so x⁻³ must equal 1/x³. Simplify x⁻² and 2⁻³ (as a fraction).
You just learned what negative exponents really mean! Tomorrow we'll combine every rule from this week into one problem.

objectives: Explain why this follows from the quotient rule
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review this week's rules so far briefly.
2. Introduce the negative-exponent rule using the x²/x⁵ reasoning from both the quotient rule and direct expansion.
3. Have the child simplify x⁻² and 2⁻³.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's combined-rules review.
differentiationTips: Struggling: work through x²/x⁵ by fully expanding and cancelling (x·x)/(x·x·x·x·x) = 1/x³ to make the reciprocal idea concrete, not just algebraic
Ready for more: ask the child to simplify a mixed expression like x⁻³·x⁵ using both the negative-exponent and product rules together
This is often the hardest of the week's rules to internalize — grounding it in direct expansion, not just the shortcut, pays off
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses Algebra 1 standards on properties of exponents, extending Common Core Grade 8 standard 8.EE.1 to negative exponents.

generationData.instructions: Simplify each expression as a fraction.
